Hand both to the artifact service's subscribe endpoint; when that service POSTs to the URL, the request body is delivered into this conversation as a <webhook-payload> message and wakes the session if idle. The signing secret inside sealed_secret is encrypted to the artifact service — it cannot be read, used, or leaked from this conversation, and only the artifact service can sign deliveries with it. A watch ends when the session ends, so call watch_url again after resuming to get a fresh one. Use this when asked to be notified when something external changes (for example, a subscribed artifact is republished). To stop, call unwatch_url with the returned trigger_id.

## Claude_Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/fortress/.claude/skills/fortress-repo

# Working in the Fortress revival repository

The team at Sun Labs built the Fortress language from 2003 to 2012 and left it unfinished. This repository finishes their design from what they left: the code, the specification and the papers. The goal is the model program, microGPT, compiled to JVM bytecode and running fast.

**curator**
: Person in charge of this restoration.

**brief**
: Instructions that you were launched with. It gives your mission.

**original tree**
: What the team left in this repository: the code, the specification, the papers and their git history. On disk, it is everything outside `explorations/`, `research/`, `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/`.

**record**
: Project's memory: the files under `explorations/` that hold what the project has established, decided and measured (below).

**walk**
: Interpreter, and the default command of `bin/fortress`: `bin/fortress P.fss` is the same as `bin/fortress walk P.fss`.

**compiled path**
: Other way to run a program: `bin/fortress compile P.fss` writes JVM bytecode, and `bin/fortress run P` runs it.

**model program**
: microGPT, the program by which the revival is measured. It has two programs: the flat program, which the record calls C4 (`explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss`), and the APL program (`explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptApl.fss`). Each has a quick check beside it, `MicroGptFlatQuick.fss` and `MicroGptAplQuick.fss`. A model line is a source line of either program.

**one library**
: Interpreter's library, which both paths use after the switch-over (below).

**component**
: Unit of Fortress code, in a `.fss` file of its own name. A component implements the apis that it exports, and uses the apis that it imports.

**api**
: Interface, in a `.fsi` file of its own name.

**area**
: One part of the system: the interpreter, the compiled path (the checker, the code generator and the run time), the library, or the specification.

**base**
: Commit that your work starts from.

**gate**
: Full check of a tree before it lands, when a brief asks for it. To land a tree is to commit it to `main` and push `main`.

**harness**
: Suites' own test runner. Each test is a whole Fortress program, not a JUnit test of a Java class. The harness runs the program and checks the result, as LLVM's lit does for Swift's test suite. `harness-one.sh` and `junit.sh` run it on the files that you name.

**building**
: Normal mode of work where you carry out the mission of your brief. You take the facts and the curator's decisions in the record as given.

**exploring**
: Mode of work for a question that the record does not settle. You gather evidence, first in the record and then in the original tree. You add what you found to the record, and then go back to building.

You work with three things: your brief, the record and the original tree. Building happens in one area at a time, so this skill has one part for each area.

## How a program runs

Walk and the compiled path share the parser and the phases below. After those, they share almost no code, so a fix on one path does not reach the other. If you edit a phase that both paths run, run your test on both paths. If you record a defect that the record does not hold, and its program can run on the other path, run it there too. Say in the ledger row which paths show the defect. The Java and Scala paths in this skill are under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/`.

### The phases

Each path runs these phases on each component, in this order (`compiler/phases/PhaseOrder.java`):

1. Parse the source into a syntax tree. This tree is the only form of the program, from the parser to the bytecode.
2. Bind each name to its declaration.
3. Expand the DSL grammars that the component imports (`references/build-and-caches.md`).
4. Check the static types. Walk's phase list holds this phase, but walk switches it off.
5. Desugar: comprehensions and big operators become calls, and getters and setters become methods.
6. Mark each call of an overloaded name.

Walk then interprets the tree. The tree has no static types, so walk finds a type error only at run time, as a failed dispatch. A program that runs under walk can be ill-typed, unlike in Java or Scala.

`fortress compile` runs the same phases with the static type checker, in Scala, switched on. Before the checker, it folds integer literals. After the phases, the code generator writes JVM bytecode into a jar. A type error stops the compile.

Each path has its own library today. At the switch-over, the compiled path moves onto the interpreter's library, and the compiler's prelude, three files of its library, is deleted (`references/compiler.md`). The compiled checker already finds no error in the interpreter's library. For the `FortressLibrary` component, the count stage shows this as a total of 0 (`references/compiler.md`). The switch-over waits for walk's natives: each function that the interpreter's library binds with `builtinPrimitive` (`references/interpreter.md`, "Natives") must first have a binding that the compiled path runs.

### The compiled run time

`fortress run` compiles no Fortress source. It runs the jars of the program and of the library on the JVM. A jar holds JVM class files:

- the component's functions, objects and traits;
- its closures;
- one dispatch method for each overloaded name. It tests the run-time types of all the arguments, from the most specific declaration to the least specific. Walk also chooses at run time.

A generic declaration is compiled once, as a template class. The first time that a program uses an instantiation, such as `Box[\RR64\]`, the class loader makes its class. It copies the template's bytecode, puts in the static arguments, and loads the result. A static argument is a type, or a size as a descriptor from `RTTIsize.of`. These classes are never on disk. C# specialises generics in this way. Java erases them.

The class loader is code of this tree that the revival changes, so a failure while a class loads can be its defect (`references/compiler.md`).

HotSpot, the JVM's compiler, then compiles the hot bytecode to machine code. A number is a boxed object, also inside a specialised class: `RR64` is the class `FRR64`. An array is a library object, read and written through its `get` and `put` methods.

### The caches

A run keeps the results of its phases in the caches, so that a later run can reuse them. The caches are folders in `default_repository/caches/`, or in a private caches folder that a run names. An entry is one file in a cache, written for one source file.

- `interpreter_parsed_cache/`: walk's parsed tree of each file, `X-<hash>.tfi` for an api and `X-<hash>.tfs` for a component.
- `interpreter_cache/`: walk's tree of each component after the phases. Walk loads it back and interprets it. The entry is a text dump of the tree. It starts `(Component @"/home/user/fortress/Library/FlatString.fss" ...`.
- `analyzed_cache/`: the results of the phases that `fortress compile` reuses.
- `bytecode_cache/`: one jar for each compiled component.

In the first three caches, `<hash>` is a hash of the source's absolute path, and the entry holds that path. So the entries of a tree copied to another path must be renamed and rewritten. `explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh` does this (`references/worktrees.md`).

`references/build-and-caches.md` says when a run reuses an entry, and when the build empties the caches.

### Parallelism and mutable state

Fortress evaluates in parallel by default, not in Java's left-to-right order. The iterations of a `for` loop, the elements of a tuple, and the arguments and operands of a call can run at once. A loop is sequential only if every generator is `seq(...)`. The parallel parts run as tasks on a work-stealing pool, the fork/join pool of Doug Lea (a `java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool`). `FORTRESS_THREADS` sets its number of threads. Tasks, transactions and the pool are built twice, independently: for walk in `interpreter/evaluator/tasks/`, and for the compiled path in `runtimeSystem/`.

`x = e` declares an immutable variable. `var x: T = e` and `x: T := e` declare a mutable one, and `x := e` assigns to it (`Specification/basic/variables.tex`). These are Scala's `val` and `var`, or Swift's `let` and `var`. A field is immutable unless it is declared with `var`. A `value` object has only immutable fields and value semantics, like a Swift `struct`.

Parallel code stays free of races in these ways:

- Most data is immutable.
- A big operator, such as `SUM` or `BIG MAX`, combines the results of its tasks, as OpenMP's reduction clause does. No task writes a shared accumulator. The specification's reduction variables are not built.
- A write to shared state goes inside an `atomic` block. This is software transactional memory, like Haskell's `atomically` (`Specification/basic/evaluation/parallelism.tex`). The programmer writes `atomic`; the compiler adds none.
- Tasks can write different elements of one array in parallel (`Specification/basic/memory-model.tex`, "Programming Discipline").

So `acc := acc + x` inside a parallel `for`, with no `atomic`, is a race. The suites run at four threads, once each, so a race can show in them. A passing run does not prove that there is none.

Inside an `atomic` block, the compiled code tracks each mutable variable that the block reads or writes (`references/compiler.md`).

## Fortress as a language

Each point below corrects an assumption from a language that you know. `references/tests-writing.md` gives the form of a program.

- **Dispatch is on every argument, at run time.** A call chooses among overloads by the run-time types of all its arguments, as in Julia, not by static types as in Java. The checker accepts two overloads only if their parameter types exclude each other, one is strictly more specific, or a third covers their meet. The more specific one's return type must fit the other's. Walk checks part of this at load.
- **Functional methods.** A method with `self` among its parameters is called `f(x)`, not `x.f()`. It overloads with top-level functions. Most operators are declared so: `opr +(self, other: T): T`. A functional method's name is reserved in every program that imports it, so do not name a variable after it. One type must not have a dotted and a functional method of the same name.
- **Traits and objects, no classes.** A trait has methods and abstract fields, and extends several traits. An object is a leaf. `excludes {A, B}` says that no value has both types. `comprises {A, B}` says that every value has a listed type, near Scala's `sealed`. No type may extend two instantiations of one generic trait. This exclusion rule is why the number types are flat (below).
- **Static parameters.** They are written `[\T\]`, and `[i]` indexes. Their kinds are types, sizes (`nat` is an `NN32` value, `int` a `ZZ32`), `bool` and `opr`. Generics are invariant: there is no `+T` or `-T`. An unbounded type parameter is bounded by `Any`, which holds tuples, functions and `()`, as `Object` does not. A type parameter that a call does not fix takes its bound. Under walk, one whose bound names the parameter itself stays open, and every value passes it. Walk instantiates a reduction or a comprehension without static arguments at the type declared for its value: a local variable's type, or a top-level or local function's return type. Without one, it uses the join, the least common supertype, of its elements' run-time types. Some other cases still get the empty type `Bottom` under walk (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Static parameters").
- **Numbers are siblings, not a tower.** `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR32` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`. None is a subtype of another, unlike Haskell's classes or Java's widening. A wider type declares a `coerce` from each narrower one. A conversion never changes which declaration runs when one already fits. Overflow raises `IntegerOverflow`. The algebra is self-typed traits, such as `AdditiveGroup[\T\]` with `+`, not monoids over an operator parameter. `references/library.md` gives the rest: ranges, wrapping, `SUM`.
- **Loops and reductions are library code.** `for`, comprehensions and `SUM` call the library's generators and reductions (`references/library.md`).
- **Juxtaposition is an operator, and whitespace counts.** `f x` applies a function. Otherwise juxtaposition is an operator that the library overloads: `2 x` multiplies, and `"a" "b"` concatenates. How three juxtaposed items group depends on their types, unlike in Haskell. An infix operator has whitespace on both sides or on neither: `a -b` is a static error. Precedence is partial: `a + b ∪ c` needs parentheses.
- **Specified, but not built:** dimensions and units, `property` declarations, regions and complex numbers. Some constructs run only under walk (`references/compiler.md`).

## The record

The record's main files:

- `explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md`: the curator's decisions.
- `explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md`: what is established about the original tree. Each fact names its test and points to the report that holds its detail.
- `explorations/coordinator/INDEX.md`: one line for each note under `explorations/`.
- `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`, the gap ledger: the known gaps, one row each.

Read a slice of the record with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh`. `references/records.md` lists its queries.

## When to explore

Switch from building to exploring when you meet one of these:

- A gap: something missing or broken that the record does not know.
- A conflict: two of the team's sources disagree, and no decision of the curator says which one is correct. The team's sources are the specification, the papers, the library and the implementations.
- New evidence against a decision of the curator. Evidence is new only if the decision did not use it. Your own view of the evidence that it used is not new evidence.

When you switch, load `references/exploring.md`. It says which choices are yours and which go to the curator.

## Rules for every task

- Carry out the curator's decisions as the record states them.
- If the record does not settle a question that your work meets, switch to exploring.
- Cite a source for each claim that you write: your brief, an entry of the record, or a primary source (the code, the specification, the papers or a command's output).
- Reproduce a behaviour before you explain it: run a command that shows it, unless your brief cites the command's output.
- When you probe or debug, change one thing at a time, so that each result has one cause.
- Write the test before the fix for every edit of source code in the original tree. Add the test to the test suite and see it fail through the harness. Then make the fix and see the test pass. An edit of the specification or the documentation has no test (`references/tests-writing.md`).
- Assert every value that matters inside the test, with the harness's own checks (`references/tests-writing.md`), and take the suite's pass or fail as the result. Do not compare the output of a whole run of tests with a saved copy, and do not add expected-output files. The gate's comparisons, and a comparison of outputs that your brief asks for, are the exceptions (`references/gate.md`, "Comparing with an earlier run").
- Take the tree that you start from as passing: its suites passed before it landed. Do not run them to check that. Start with your own failing test.
- Reuse each result of a build, a suite, a stage of the gate, a test or a measurement that your brief cites or that your own work ran. Cite it. Run it again only after the code changes. Running a new program is not a repeat.
- Before you investigate a defect, or edit a file of the original tree, look for its rows in the gap ledger, with the queries of `references/records.md`, "Reading the record".
- After your fix, run your own tests. Run a whole suite where `references/tests-running.md`, "When to run a whole suite", asks for it, and nowhere else.
- Set up each Bash call as `references/build-and-caches.md` says, because every call starts a new shell.
- After an edit, take the step that `references/build-and-caches.md` gives for the kind of file that you edited.
- Run long commands (a build, a suite) in the background with a log under your tree's `tmp/`, and poll the log (`references/session.md`). Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: if the Bash tool's time limit stops the command, it shows nothing.
- Before you design a change to the library, study how the library already does the same kind of thing, and follow its way (`references/library.md`).
- Do not claim credit for the revival anywhere in a committed file. If git does not record who wrote something, reconstruct the authorship from the history. Do not guess it.
- Commit only the paths that you wrote. Do not commit scratch: logs, captured output, probe programs. Do not rename a file to get it past `.gitignore`. Each agent's transcript keeps how the work was done (`references/committing.md`).
- End your work with a report. List in it the defects that you found, your decisions, and the points that your brief asks for. Put a question for the curator in it as a decision not taken (`references/records.md`).

## The parts

Load the parts below that your task touches before you run the query of the record that your brief gives. The parts give the words that you need to understand what the query prints.

The parts, in the order that work meets them:

- Setting up each call, building, the caches, what to rebuild after an edit: `references/build-and-caches.md`
- The Bash tool and its timeout, long commands and polling, waits and the prompt cache, stopping processes, interrupts and stops of the session's process, the automatic permission check: `references/session.md`
- The base and its build, worktrees seeded from it, the old code beside the new: `references/worktrees.md`
- The build failing, JDKs, scalac and ASM traps, generated sources: `references/toolchain.md`
- The interpreter area: walk's code (`interpreter/`), where a fix of walk belongs, its checks at load, its natives, running programs under walk, the microGPT check: `references/interpreter.md`
- The compiled area: the checker, the code generator, the run time, compiled runs, the `fortress` commands, the checker's time after a change: `references/compiler.md`
- The library area (`Library/`, `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`): `references/library.md`
- The specification area (`Specification/`), Appendix I, citing it: `references/specification.md`
- How revived Fortress differs from the team's Fortress and from the languages that you know; read it whole, after this file, before work: `references/revival-changes.md`
- Exploring: where to search, what to record and report, which choices are yours: `references/exploring.md`
- Writing a test: `.test` keys, `XXX` expected failures and their promotion, refusals at load, how a defect that you found is recorded: `references/tests-writing.md`
- Running one test, a few, or a whole suite, and when to run a whole suite; what runs outside the gate: `references/tests-running.md`
- The gate: what it runs and writes, the atomic runs, the ladder regression, comparing with an earlier run: `references/gate.md`
- Committing and pushing: `references/committing.md`
- What every report holds and where it goes, findings and points to report; POSITIONS, FACTS and the gap ledger; the queries of the record and when to run each; writing the ledger with `ledger.py`; the repository's history: `references/records.md`
- This cloud platform (the machine, the disk, the network, the platform's stops, the transcript backup, a lost container): the `cloud-container` skill.

A task usually needs several parts, and every task needs `revival-changes.md`, read whole before work, and `records.md`, for its queries and its report. For example, a fix of walk needs `build-and-caches.md`, `session.md`, `worktrees.md`, `interpreter.md`, `tests-writing.md`, `tests-running.md` and `committing.md`. An edit of the library needs the same parts and `library.md`.

`references/sources.md` gives the source of each fact in these parts. Use it only to maintain this skill. Do not load it for a task.

native component FlatString

import String.{maxLeafSize, concatAndBalanceIfNecessary, CatString, spaces}
import Stream.{...}

export FlatString


private language="java"
private package="com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim"

lineSeparator: String = LineSeparator()

private natLineSeparator(): String = builtinPrimitive(
            "com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.Writer$LineSeparator")

private LineSeparator(): String =do
    ignore(FlatString); (* This initializes the constructor for FlatString
                   before its type is used (in the next line). *)
    natLineSeparator()
  end

object FlatString extends { String, DelegatedIndexed⟦Char, ZZ32⟧ }
    getter size() : ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$Size")
    getter asExprString() : String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$ToString")
    getter asFlatString(): String = self
    getter asString(): String = self
    getter asDebugString(): String = asDebugStringIndented(0)
    getter depth():ZZ32 = 0

    (* With the help of trait DelegatedIndex, this defines our generate method *)
    getter generator() : Generator⟦Char⟧ =
        self.indices.map⟦Char⟧(fn (i:ZZ32):Char ⇒ self.get(i))

    getter isBalanced():Boolean = true
    getter isAlmostBalanced():Boolean = true
    getter isExtremelyUnbalanced():Boolean = false

    balanced():String = self

    opr |self| : ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$Size")

    uncheckedSubstring(r1: Range⟦ZZ32⟧) : String = do
    (* We could build a subString node here, but not until everything is working,
        because that will introduce
       SubString objects into code that may still expect FlatStrings.
       As written, this method always answers a FlatString.
       In any case, the FlatString object supports substring without copying*)
        assert((r1 ∩ self.bounds).isEmpty, r1.isEmpty,
                    "Empty substring of non-empty string")
        if r1.isEmpty then ""
        else self.javaSubstr(r1.left.get, r1.right.get + 1)    (* Java substr's endIndex is one past the last character *)
        end
    end

    opr =(self, other: FlatString): Boolean =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$Eq")
    opr <(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) < 0
    opr <=(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) ≤ 0
    opr >(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) > 0
    opr >=(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) ≥ 0
    opr CMP(self, other: FlatString): TotalComparison =  self.cmp(other) CMP 0
    opr CMP(self, other:String):TotalComparison = INVERSE (other CMP self)
    opr CASE_INSENSITIVE_CMP(self, other:FlatString): TotalComparison =
      self.cicmp(other) CMP 0
    opr CASE_INSENSITIVE_CMP(self, other:String): TotalComparison = INVERSE (other CASE_INSENSITIVE_CMP self)

    (** get skips bounds checking. **)
    get(i:ZZ32): Char =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$Index")
    cmp(other:FlatString): ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$Cmp")
    cicmp(other:FlatString): ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$CICmp")
    javaSubstr(lo:ZZ32,hi:ZZ32): String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$Substr")
    javaSubstr(lo:ZZ32): String = javaSubstr(lo, self.size)
    javaIndexOf(c:Char): ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$IndexOf")
    flatConcat(self, b:FlatString):String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$Concat")
    flatConcat(self, b:Char):String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$Concat")
    javaRegExpMatches(m:FlatString): Boolean =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$javaRegExpMatches")
    javaRegExpSplit(m:FlatString, i:ZZ32): String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$javaRegExpSplit")

    indexOf(c:Char): Maybe⟦ZZ32⟧ = do
        i = javaIndexOf(c)
        if i = -1 then Nothing⟦ZZ32⟧ else Just⟦ZZ32⟧(i) end
      end

    verify():() = do
        assert(self.depth, 0, self)
    end

    asDebugStringIndented(indent: ZZ32): String =
        spaces(indent) || "J" |self| "/" self.depth ":" self

    opr ∈(c:Char, self): Boolean = self.javaIndexOf(c) ≠ -1

    rangeContains(r: Range⟦ZZ32⟧, c: Char):Boolean = self.javaIndexOf(c) ∈ self.bounds[r]

    (** The operator %||% with at least one String argument converts to string and
        concatenates **)
    opr ||(self, b:FlatString): String = do
        if b.isEmpty then self
        elif self.size + b.size > maxLeafSize then
             (* Since both self and b have depth 0, balancing can't be necessary *)
            CatString(self, b)
        else
            flatConcat(self, b)
        end
      end

    opr ||(self, b:String):String = do
        if self.isEmpty then b
        elif b.isEmpty then self
        elif self.size + b.size > maxLeafSize then
            concatAndBalanceIfNecessary(self, b)
        else
            typecase b.asFlatString of
                f:FlatString ⇒ flatConcat(self, f)
                f:String ⇒ concatAndBalanceIfNecessary(self, b)
            end
        end
    end

    opr ||(self, b:Char): String =
        if |self| ≥ maxLeafSize then
            concatAndBalanceIfNecessary(self, b.asString)
        else
            flatConcat(self, b)
        end

    splitWithOffsets():ZeroIndexed⟦(ZZ32, String)⟧ = Nothing⟦(ZZ32, String)⟧
    split():Generator⟦String⟧ = Nothing⟦String⟧

    writeOn(stream: WriteStream): () = stream.write(self)

end FlatString

end

<!-- The clarity pass's corrections to chunk c1 (P-7, P-27, P-146, P-153, P-154, P-12, P-17), after the cold read and the check: each sentence that findings.md names, corrected from its ground, with every other sentence kept as POSITIONS holds it at 5da8144e4. -->

# Chunk c1: corrections from the findings

Only the sentences that a finding names change. Every other sentence is the text of POSITIONS at `5da8144e4`, word for word. The cold read and the check found more faults in unchanged sentences. No finding names them, so they stay, and each entry lists them under "Left for a later pass".

## P-7

- P-7 **The goal is to finish what the designers intended, measured by one program, microGPT, compiled to JVM bytecode and running fast.** What the designers intended is judged by the specification in `Specification/`: the team's Working Draft of February 2011, as the revival revises it, with the Types chapter of the team's 2012 restart cited beside it (P-25). The revival revises the specification to reconcile contradictions: where the team's later work, in the compiler or in the papers on types, contradicts the original text, the text is updated to follow that work (P-26: the type group's later word wins). The language is not redesigned. The specification is a living document that states each change that the revival makes (P-95 says how a change is recorded). A pure-Java microGPT is the baseline that compiled microGPT is measured against: the optimal result, the one to aim at.

Meaning: unchanged. The text is unchanged.

Sources: the finding's only ground is the foundations judge's reasoning (`judgement.md`, tenet 1). So the text stays. The sentence at issue is close to the curator's own words: "when later work in compiler or type papers contradict the original spec, we updated it to match the current state of the implementation in the revival." (2026-10-12T23:15:30Z). The cold reader took it to mean that any compiler code counts, which is the misreading that the finding names.

Question for the curator: "the team's later work, in the compiler" covers two kinds of work. One is a rule that the team's checker enforces on purpose. The other is code that works around a JVM limit or a gap in the checker. Should P-7 say only that the text follows the team's later word, and leave to P-26 which work in the compiler counts? The pending rewrite in `evidence/rewrite/combined.apply` already has that form: "P-26 says what counts as the team's later word, and when the team's work in the compiler counts."

Left for a later pass: the pure-Java baseline is not yet written, and the entry lost the line that said so (PLAN phase 6). The cold reader could not tell whether a gap in the texts counts as a contradiction; P-8 covers gaps.

## P-27

- P-27 **Whoever extends the library follows the library's own practice.** What microGPT invented goes into the standard library, in the library's own style. Whoever extends the library first studies how it does the same kind of thing, and follows that pattern; exclusion, for one, is all over it. He had to find the diagonal's override himself (P-88) because that study was skipped. No fix is designed from the specification alone or from a workaround on the user's side. This rule governs how the library is extended. It does not choose between two of the team's designs of the language, such as the self type as the interpreter's library and the compiler's prelude write it: the team's later word, dated against the texts, decides between them (P-26).

Meaning: one change, from the finding. The title was "The library's own practice is the standard." Read alone, it reads as a rule for every question of design. The new title states the body's scope, and two new sentences state the limit.

Sources:
- The trap test, scenario 2 (`evidence/trap-test/grades.md`, section 4, "POSITIONS 27"). A reader took this entry as the ground to drop a change that copied the compiler's prelude, because the library never had that form. The grader's fact: P-27 "does not decide between two of the team's own designs; the dated later word does". The last sentence keeps "dated", because today's P-26 has no dating test.
- The limit holds for designs of the language only. The foundations judgement uses P-27 to choose between two forms that the team built for the natives, `builtinPrimitive` and `import java` (tenet 8), and that choice is outside the language. The example names a design of the language, the self type, so that "the library's text" is not read as the specification's text.
- The curator's words behind the body (2026-09-19T18:31:44Z) speak only of extending the library: "use those patterns for extending the standard library in the native way".

Question for the curator: the cold reader took "What microGPT invented goes into the standard library" as a duty to move every one of microGPT's own forms into the library. Your later words narrow it: "As long as the extensions that we did have a precedent in the library itself, I, I'm fine with that." (2026-09-20T07:20:24Z), and "I would at most admit to wanting to extend the standard library for the needs of C4 if it was missing an obvious extension" (2026-10-09T05:20:34Z). Should the sentence read: "An extension that microGPT needed goes into the standard library only where the library has a precedent for it, such as an operation that a lower-dimensional array has and a higher one lacks"?

Knock-on, for the coordinator: P-84 glosses its pointer as "(P-27, the library's own practice is the standard)", the old title that the finding faults, and so does `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/sources.md:224`. P-84 is not in this chunk; its gloss should change to the new title when this entry lands.

Left for a later pass: "He" has no antecedent (it is the curator), and the sentence tells how the rule came about. "Exclusion, for one, is all over it" means the library's `excludes` clauses. "A workaround on the user's side" means a workaround in the program that meets the gap.

## P-146

- P-146 **In a self-typed trait, the compiled checker types `self` in the method bodies as also being the implementing type.** A self-typed trait is a trait `C[\X\]` whose parameter `X` extends `C[\X\]`, such as `Integral[\I extends Integral[\I\]\]`. In its method bodies, `self` has the type `C[\X\] & X`. The method signatures keep the plain trait type, because the proofs of the POPL 2019 paper on multiple dispatch (Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu) assume that no declared type holds a type parameter inside an intersection. Only the overloading check's exclusion test reads `self` in a signature as `C[\X\] & X` (P-157). The checker refuses a type that extends such a trait at another type, since an extender must be a subtype of the static argument that it gives: `object Bad extends Integral[\ZZ32\]` is refused, because `Bad` is not a `ZZ32`. Scala has the same rule for self types. The library's text gains no self type and no `comprises` clause, and walk is unchanged. The rule accepts every self-typed method body of the library except `Integral`'s `numerator`, which each integer type declares instead. Why: the team's later texts point, if weakly, toward the rule, and peer languages share it. The compiler's prelude writes the self type as a `comprises T` clause instead, and that form does not bind the library: Naden's write-up on the Return Type Rule (P-26 names it), later than the team's last edits of that clause, puts the self type in bounds only, the form `X extends C[\X\]` that the library writes. F-225 states the rule as built and holds the dates.

Meaning: one change, from findings (a) and (b). The "Why" was: "the checker reads the library as the team wrote it, as P-44 does for the closure of `AnyIntegral`, by one rule that peer languages share."

- Finding (a): that reason led a reader to drop a change that copied the prelude's `comprises T` only because the library never had it (trap test, scenario 2; `grades.md`, section 4, "POSITIONS 146"). The ground is the date. Naden's write-up of 2012-08-31 (`8015b17f4`) says that the idiom "should be ... a separate construct which cannot be used as a first class type, but instead only in bounds" (`Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex:626-630`). Steele put `comprises T` on `StandardTotalOrder` on 2012-06-05 (`655e65d53`) and removed its F-bound on 2012-06-06 (`59fdeff62`); `Equality`'s clause is older. So the text says "the team's last edits of that clause", not that Steele introduced it. F-225 holds the dates (finding (b): F-225 completed the idiom's history at `0d2206c5f`).
- The curator's reason: "option 1 is more in line with weak signal from repo and has precedent in other languages as well" (2026-10-13T23:32:10Z). It answers the coordinator's turn of 23:24:28Z, "How clear is the later team signal?", which listed Welterweight, the Types chapter and Naden, and called the signal "only indirect for option 1". So the signal he named is the team's later texts, weakly for the rule. The first sentence of the "Why" now says that. The first round's "the library's own form" was the coordinator's reading, and it restated the ground that finding (a) faults.
- The comparison with P-44 left with the old clause. It was the coordinator's reason, not the curator's (scout report, section 2).

Sources of the other sentences: the text at `5da8144e4`.

Question for the curator: none. The check settled the first round's question from the coordinator's turn that the curator answered.

Left for a later pass: the checker also accepts a trait whose parameter is bounded by a self-typed trait that it extends at that parameter, as the team's `Containment` mixins are, a default of the coordinator's (F-225). Read to the letter, the extender sentence would refuse that case.

## P-153

- P-153 **The integer power splits on the base: an integer base gives an integer or raises an error, and a float or rational base gives the fraction.** Each integer type's `^` returns its own type at every exponent. At a negative exponent, the bases 1 and -1 give their exact power, a base of 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and any other base raises `IntegerOverflow`. A program that wants a fraction writes a float or rational base, as in `2.0^(-1)`. Why: the Working Draft's power, which gives a rational at a signed exponent, was never built on either path. The only power with an integer result type that the team built is the compiler's prelude's, which gives `ZZ32`, `NN32` and `NN64` each a power of its own type at every exponent. Overloads choose by type, and no type tells a negative exponent from a non-negative one, since a signed integer or a numeral can be either. So the split is on the base, and the sign of the exponent is tested at run time, as the library tests a value's sign everywhere (P-80, run-time sign tests in place of sign-refined types). Row 441: the same rule on the compiled path, whose own powers give 0 at a negative exponent and a raw Java exception at a base of 0, and overflow silently or with a raw Java exception (row 523).

Meaning: one change, from the finding. The first sentence of the "Why" was: "the team's later code gives an integer power the type of its integer base at a signed exponent (P-26, the team's later work outweighs the specification's early text)." It called the compiled path's code the team's later word on the language. The judge's sound ground (`judgement.md`, section 3) is that the Working Draft's rational power was never built on either path, and that the prelude's rule is the only one implemented, the same for the three integer types. The two new sentences state these facts. The second says "with an integer result type", since the interpreter's library also built a power, typed `RR64`.

Sources: the integer-power judgement, section 2.3 (`explorations/reviews/integer-power-fable-judgement.md`). The interpreter's library typed every integer power `RR64`, and its natives gave an integer at a non-negative exponent and a float at a negative one (`Int.java:222-231`). The compiler's prelude declares `opr ^(self, other:ZZ32): ZZ32`, `opr ^(self, other:NN32):NN32` and `opr ^(self, other:NN64):NN64` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:267`, `:326`, `:385`, checked). Prelude sweep, section 2.2, row P5. The other sentences: the text at `5da8144e4`.

Question for the curator: the judge reads the prelude's rule as an implementation choice in a gap of the language's texts, which the goal (P-8) lets decide. That step is the judge's reasoning only, so the entry does not state it. Do you take it as the reason? The rewrite note lists P-153's "Why" as owed against the new P-26 (`rewrite-results.md`, "Still owed").

Left for a later pass: the "Row 441" sentence has no verb; row 441 tracks the compiled path's departure from this rule, and row 523 their overflow. The entry does not say which exponents `^` takes; the interpreter's library takes any integer or numeral exponent.

## P-154

- P-154 **A list is ordered only where its element type is totally ordered.** The library's `List` extends its lexicographic order only where its element type extends `StandardTotalOrder` (conditional extension, P-151). Floats and `QQ` are only partially ordered, since NaN, and `QQ`'s 0/0, compare with nothing. So on the compiled checker a list of floats or of `QQ` has no order: no `<`, `CMP` or the other comparisons, though its `=` stays. A pair of floats stays ordered: the curator accepted that mismatch as a cost of the list rule. The tuples' own rule is not decided here. No lexicographic trait over partially ordered elements is added now: the team never wrote one, and the case touches neither the distance to the switch-over nor microGPT. Why: the two lexicographic traits of an unfinished library draft of the team's (`Library/incomplete/advanced/Fortress.PartialTotalOrders.fss:117-140`) both bound the element by a total order, and conditional extension is a `where` form that the team wrote (P-151). The draft is not shown to be later than the specification's sentence that lets a list's order be partial where its elements' order is, so it does not count as the team's later word (P-26). Row 774: walk's half, since walk still gives every list an order.

Meaning: one change, from the finding. The "Why" called the draft "the team's later code" and ranked it by P-26. Git cannot show the draft to be later. The new text keeps the fact, the bound in the draft's two traits, and says that the draft does not count as the team's later word.

Sources:
- Git. The finding found the file's first commit under its path to be the root snapshot `5a68404fd` (2012-07-19). Under its older path, `StandardLibrary/advanced/Fortress.PartialTotalOrders.fss`, both traits and their bound are already in `eeda9cd95` (2007-09-26), so the draft dates from 2007 or before. The specification's sentence, "which may be partial or total depending on whether the ordering of the elements is partial or total" (`Specification/advanced-lib/algebraic-constraints.tex:519-522`), is traced only to `d8859d236` (2009-10-20). So neither text is shown to be the later one.

That was false: the team's library declares `LexicographicOrder[\T extends LexicographicOrder[\T,E\],E\]` with no bound on `E`, and `List` extended it for every element type (`5a68404fd`: `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1196`, `Library/List.fsi:67`). The bound on `E` is the revival's (`372b9bf6a`). The text now names the draft's two traits only, as the old text did.
- The other sentences: the text at `5da8144e4`.

Question for the curator: you agreed to the recommendation "The team's later word outweighs its early text (P-26)" (2026-10-20T06:18Z). With that ground gone, the decision rests on the team's draft and on your own reason: no new trait, since the case is off the path to a compiled microGPT. Note too that the team's own library gave every list a total order, with no bound on the element. Does the decision stand on these grounds?

Left for a later pass: "A pair of floats stays ordered" describes today's behaviour, which the curator accepted; it is not a decision on tuples. "Extends its lexicographic order" should name the trait `LexicographicOrder`.

## P-12

- P-12 **After the switch-over, walk runs the compiled type checker on its programs, and then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts.** The curator wants the checker usable on the programs that walk runs. Today `fortress typecheck` checks a program only against the compiler's prelude, so it is no check of walk's programs (F-9 holds this fact). Walk is not changed for this before the switch-over. After it, walk runs the checker on its programs and so gains their static types. Walk then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts, in place of its choice on the run-time value (P-59, walk's choice of coercions until the switch-over). The step has three parts, and its size is unmeasured. First, walk must run with the Scala checker on; today it runs with it off. Second, walk must evaluate the `CoercionInvocation` nodes that the checker inserts, for which it has no case today (F-9 holds both facts). Third, the components that walk's programs import must be cleared of the checker's errors, each before this step or before the first program that needs it (F-290 counts them).

Meaning: one addition, from the finding. "Walk runs the checker on its programs" understated the step. The four new sentences name its three parts and say that its size is unmeasured. The decision does not change. The third part says when the components are cleared, so that it is not read as waiting for the switch-over: it changes the library, not walk.

Sources: the judgement, tenet 9, by code reading. With Scala off, `StaticChecker.java:228-229` throws "The Java version of the type checker is gone now." (checked). No file under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/` names `CoercionInvocation` (checked). F-9 states both facts, with row 833. F-290 counts 624 errors in 30 of the library's 40 other components, measured once. The third part's timing: the judgement, section 2 ("the 40 are P-12's"), and section 7 under P-33 ("place the 40 other components before P-12's step or the first program that needs each, not before the switch-over"). The other sentences: the text at `5da8144e4`.

Question for the curator: none.

## P-17

- P-17 **Unboxed doubles and arrays of unboxed doubles are required: without them the revival misses its point.** Why: a language meant for high performance cannot box its numbers. The specification states the same intent: its chapter on objects lets an implementation freely copy value objects, among them floating-point numbers, and its chapter on memory sequences makes a `LinearSequence` of a value type a sequence of "unboxed" values. Today the code generator boxes every number: an `RR64` value is an object of the class `FRR64`. In Java models of microGPT's three array kernels, the dot product, the matrix product and the row lift, boxing is the main cost (F-11 holds the measurement). How arrays store doubles, as `double[]`, is P-84's decision.

content.content:
# Cold read 2 of corrections/c1/clean.txt

Context read: `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/SKILL.md`, and, to look up terms, `references/compiler.md`, `references/library.md`, `references/exploring.md`, `references/records.md` and `references/interpreter.md`. I read nothing else.

The file holds seven entries, all of them positions: P-7, P-27, P-146, P-153, P-154, P-12 and P-17.

---

## P-7: the goal, and what judges the designers' intent

- **Decided:** The revival finishes the design that Fortress's designers meant, and does not redesign the language. Success is measured by one program, microGPT, compiled to JVM bytecode and running fast. The specification in `Specification/` is the measure of what the designers meant. That specification is the team's Working Draft of February 2011, as the revival revises it, read together with the Types chapter of the team's 2012 restart (P-25). The revival changes the text only to remove contradictions. Where the team's later work, in the compiler or in the type papers, contradicts the original text, the text is changed to follow the later work (P-26). The specification stays a living document that states every change the revival makes to it (P-95 says how). A microGPT written in plain Java is the baseline for the measurement: it is the best possible result, and compiled microGPT aims at it.
- **Applies:** To the whole revival, as its overall goal and as the rule for reading intent. Limits: the specification is revised only to reconcile contradictions with the team's later work, never to add new design. "The language is not redesigned."
- **Requires:** A worker judges intent by the specification. Where a later team source contradicts it, the worker follows the later source and records the change in the specification as P-95 says. A worker must not redesign the language. Performance is measured against the pure-Java microGPT.
- **Unfinished:** The goal itself: microGPT compiled and running fast. The entry gives no number for "fast" beyond "aim at" the pure-Java result.
- **Could not resolve:**
  - "the Types chapter of the team's 2012 restart": I do not know what the 2012 restart was, or where that chapter is. P-25 is cited for it. This is a gap in context, not a language concept.
  - "cited beside it": unclear wording. It does not say whether that chapter has the same authority as the Working Draft, or is only a reference read next to it. P-26 ("later word wins") suggests it outranks the draft where they disagree, but the entry does not say so.
  - "the baseline ... the optimal result, the one to aim at": unclear wording. "Baseline" usually means the floor that a result is compared up from. Here it means the ceiling. The sense can be recovered, but the word pulls the other way.
  - Where the pure-Java microGPT lives is not named. That matters only to a worker who has to run it.

## P-27: extending the library follows the library's own practice

- **Decided:** Whoever extends the library first studies how the library already does that kind of thing, then follows the same pattern. Things that microGPT had to invent for itself go into the standard library, written in the library's style. A fix is never designed only from the specification, or from a workaround on the user's side. The entry names exclusion as one pattern that runs all through the library. The rule covers only how the library is extended. It does not pick between two of the team's language designs (for example the self type, written one way by the interpreter's library and another way by the compiler's prelude). There the team's later word decides, dated against the texts (P-26).
- **Applies:** Whenever someone adds to or fixes the library, including extensions that only microGPT needs. Limit: it does not settle conflicts between team designs of the language itself.
- **Requires:** Study the library's existing practice before designing a change, and follow it. Do not design from the specification text alone. Do not design from a user-side workaround. Move microGPT's own inventions into the library.
- **Unfinished:** The entry does not say whether microGPT's inventions are already in the library or still have to be moved.
- **Could not resolve:**
  - "He had to find the diagonal's override himself (P-88)": unclear wording. "He" has no antecedent. It may mean the curator, or an earlier worker. I cannot tell who. "The diagonal's override" is a specific case I cannot identify (perhaps an override of a matrix-diagonal method). The sentence reads as a cautionary example, and it gives a worker nothing to act on without P-88.
  - "exclusion, for one, is all over it": unclear wording. It may mean `excludes` clauses on traits, or the overloading exclusion rule (SKILL: "parameter types exclude each other"). The point is presumably that the library leans on exclusion where a new design might reach for something else. Even so, a worker cannot tell what to do differently.
  - "No fix is designed ... from a workaround on the user's side": two readings. (a) A library gap must not be patched over by a workaround in the user's program (this matches `library.md`, "Fix a gap in the library, not by a workaround in the program that meets it"). (b) The library's design must not be copied from the shape of the workaround that the user wrote. "Designed from" favours (b). The library reference favours (a).
  - "What microGPT invented": I read it as helpers and types that the model program defines itself because the library lacks them. The wording is loose, but I think it is clear enough.

## P-146: how the compiled checker types `self` in a self-typed trait

- **Decided:** A self-typed trait is `C[\X\]` whose parameter `X` extends `C[\X\]`, such as `Integral[\I extends Integral[\I\]\]`. Inside its method bodies, the compiled checker types `self` as `C[\X\] & X`: both the trait and the implementing type. Method signatures keep the plain trait type, because the POPL 2019 dispatch proofs assume that no declared type puts a type parameter inside an intersection. The one exception is the overloading check's exclusion test, which reads `self` in a signature as `C[\X\] & X` (P-157). The checker refuses an extender that instantiates the trait at some other type. An extender must be a subtype of the static argument it gives, so `object Bad extends Integral[\ZZ32\]` is refused, because `Bad` is not a `ZZ32` (Scala has the same rule). The library's source is not changed: no self-type annotation and no `comprises` clause are added. Walk is unchanged. With this rule, every self-typed method body in the library type-checks except `Integral`'s `numerator`, which each integer type declares itself instead. Reasons: the team's later texts point weakly toward the rule, and peer languages share it. The compiler's prelude writes the self type as a `comprises T` clause, but that form does not bind the library. Naden's Return Type Rule write-up is later than the team's last edits of that clause, and it puts the self type only in bounds (`X extends C[\X\]`), which is how the library writes it. F-225 states the rule as built, with the dates.
- **Applies:** On the compiled checker only, to traits of the self-typed shape above. Limits: method bodies only; signatures stay plain, except inside the exclusion test. Walk is not affected.
- **Requires:** Do not add a self type or a `comprises` clause to the library's text. Do not change walk for this. Do not write signatures with `C[\X\] & X`. An extender of a self-typed trait must instantiate it at itself. Do not expect a `numerator` body in `Integral` to check; each integer type declares its own.
- **Unfinished:** Nothing is stated as unfinished. F-225 calls the rule built. The entry does not say whether walk should ever refuse `Bad`.
- **Could not resolve:**
  - "The library's text gains no self type": a language concept I lack. The skill shows no Fortress syntax for declaring a self type apart from the `comprises T` form and the bound `X extends C[\X\]`. So I am not sure what form is being ruled out, beyond the `comprises` clause, which is named.
  - "except `Integral`'s `numerator`, which each integer type declares instead": two readings. Either the library already declares `numerator` in each integer type (a fact), or a worker must move it there (a requirement). The entry also leaves open whether `Integral` keeps an abstract `numerator`.
  - "an extender must be a subtype of the static argument that it gives": the limit is unclear. The example is a concrete object. The entry does not say what happens to a generic trait that passes its own self parameter on, as in `trait T[\Y extends T[\Y\]\] extends Integral[\Y\]`. `T[\Y\]` is not a subtype of `Y`, so read literally the rule refuses it. I cannot tell whether that is meant.
  - "the team's later texts point, if weakly, toward the rule": the texts are not named here. F-225 may hold them.

## P-153: integer power, split on the base

- **Decided:** Every integer type's `^` returns that same integer type at every exponent. At a negative exponent: base 1 gives 1, base -1 gives its exact power (±1), base 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and any other base raises `IntegerOverflow`. To get a fraction, a program writes a float or rational base, as in `2.0^(-1)`. Reasons: the Working Draft's power, which gives a rational at a signed exponent, was never built on either path. The only integer-result power the team built is the compiler's prelude's, which gives `ZZ32`, `NN32` and `NN64` each a power of its own type. Overloads choose by type, and no type marks an exponent as negative (a signed integer or a numeral can be either), so the choice goes by the base's type. The exponent's sign is tested at run time, as the library tests signs everywhere (P-80).
- **Applies:** To `^` on every integer type, on both paths. Limits: the split is by the base's static type. An integer base never gives a fraction, whatever the exponent.
- **Requires:** Do not make an integer power return a rational or a float. Test the exponent's sign at run time, not through overloads or sign-refined types. Raise the named Fortress exceptions, never a raw Java exception. A test that wants a fraction uses a float or rational base.
- **Unfinished:** The compiled path. Its own powers give 0 at a negative exponent, give a raw Java exception at base 0, and overflow either silently or with a raw Java exception. Rows 441 and 523 hold this. The entry does not say whether walk's library already follows the rule.
- **Could not resolve:**
  - "Row 441: the same rule on the compiled path, whose own powers give 0 ...": unclear wording, because the sentence has no verb. I read it as "ledger row 441 is the open gap: the compiled path must get this same rule; today its powers give 0 ...". It could also be read as "row 441 records that the compiled path has this rule", which the rest of the sentence contradicts.
  - "and overflow silently or with a raw Java exception (row 523)": unclear wording. It is unclear whether overflow at a non-negative exponent belongs to row 441 with the rest, or to row 523 alone. Nor does it say which of the compiled powers overflow silently and which throw.
  - The exponent's type is not stated. Must it be the base's type, or can it be any integer (or numeral)? For `NN32` and `NN64` bases, the exponent cannot be negative if it has the base's type. The entry does not say whether those types take a signed exponent.
  - Whether `ZZ` (the unbounded integer) is among "each integer type" is not stated. I assume it is.

## P-154: a list is ordered only where its element type is totally ordered

- **Decided:** The library's `List` takes on its lexicographic order only where its element type extends `StandardTotalOrder`. It does so by conditional extension (a `where` form, P-151). Floats and `QQ` are only partially ordered, because NaN and `QQ`'s 0/0 compare with nothing. So on the compiled checker, a list of floats or of `QQ` has no `<`, `CMP` or other comparison, though `=` still works. A pair of floats stays ordered. The curator accepts that mismatch as a cost of the list rule. The rule for tuples is not decided here. No lexicographic trait over partially ordered elements is added now: the team never wrote one, and it touches neither the distance to the switch-over nor microGPT. Reasons: the two lexicographic traits in the team's unfinished draft (`Library/incomplete/advanced/Fortress.PartialTotalOrders.fss:117-140`) both bound the element by a total order, and conditional extension is a form the team wrote (P-151). The draft is not shown to be later than the specification's sentence that lets a list's order be partial where its elements' order is, so it does not count as the team's later word (P-26).
- **Applies:** To the library's `List`, on the compiled checker now. Limits: equality on lists is untouched. Tuples are outside the rule. Ordered lists over partial orders are not built now.
- **Requires:** Do not give a list of floats or of `QQ` comparisons. Do not add a partial-order lexicographic trait. Do not treat the incomplete draft as the team's later word.
- **Unfinished:** Walk's half: walk still gives every list an order (row 774). A partial lexicographic order is left for later, and so is the tuples' rule.
- **Could not resolve:**
  - "A pair of floats stays ordered ... The tuples' own rule is not decided here": two readings. (a) Pairs keep their order for good, as an accepted cost. (b) Pairs keep their order only until the tuples' rule is decided. The mention of tuples suggests that "pair" means a tuple `(RR64, RR64)`, but the library may also have a `Pair` type. I cannot tell which is meant.
  - "the specification's sentence that lets a list's order be partial where its elements' order is": unclear. The specification allows a partially ordered list of floats, and the decision gives such a list no order. So I cannot tell whether this is a revision of the specification (which P-7 says must be stated in the text) or a deferral of an unbuilt part. "No ... trait ... is added now" suggests deferral, but the entry does not say whether the specification is changed.
  - "the distance to the switch-over": a term I could not find in the skill. I read it as how much work is left before the switch-over (perhaps the checker count), but the skill does not define it.
  - "Row 774: walk's half": unclear wording, because the sentence has no verb. I read it as "ledger row 774 holds the walk part, still open".
  - `CMP`: I take it to be the three-way comparison operator. I could not confirm it in the skill.

## P-12: after the switch-over, walk runs the compiled checker and uses its coercions

- **Decided:** After the switch-over, walk runs the compiled type checker on the programs it runs, which gives them static types. Walk then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts, in place of choosing a coercion from the run-time value (P-59). The curator wants the checker usable on walk's programs. Today `fortress typecheck` checks only against the compiler's prelude, so it does not check walk's programs (F-9). Walk is not changed for this before the switch-over. The step has three parts, and its size is unmeasured: (1) walk runs with the Scala checker on, where today it is off; (2) walk evaluates the `CoercionInvocation` nodes that the checker inserts, which it has no case for today (F-9); (3) the components that walk's programs import are cleared of the checker's errors (F-290 counts them).
- **Applies:** Only after the switch-over. Before it, walk stays as it is and keeps choosing coercions at run time.
- **Requires:** Before the switch-over, a worker must not change walk to run the checker or to use static coercions. After it, the three parts are to be built. Each imported component is cleared of checker errors either before this step or before the first program that needs that component.
- **Unfinished:** All three parts. The size of the work is unmeasured.
- **Could not resolve:**
  - "each before this step or before the first program that needs it": unclear wording. Read loosely, a component may be cleared either before the whole step or later, before the first program that imports it. That second option suggests the step can land with some components still failing. But "this step" could also mean part 3 itself. The phrase "needs it" probably means "imports that component", but it might mean "needs it cleared".
  - The entry does not say what walk does with a program that the checker refuses once the checker is on. A program that runs under walk today can be ill-typed (SKILL, "The phases"). Will walk then refuse it, or warn and run it?
  - "walk's programs": which set this is (every program walk runs, or the suites and the model program) is not stated. I take it to mean every program.

## P-17: unboxed doubles and arrays of unboxed doubles are required

- **Decided:** The compiled code must keep doubles unboxed, and arrays of doubles too. Without that, the revival misses its point. Reasons: a language meant for high performance cannot box its numbers. The specification states the same intent: its chapter on objects lets an implementation copy value objects, floats among them, freely, and its chapter on memory sequences makes a `LinearSequence` of a value type a sequence of unboxed values. Today the code generator boxes every number (an `RR64` is an `FRR64` object). In Java models of microGPT's three array kernels (dot product, matrix product, row lift), boxing is the main cost (F-11). How arrays store doubles, as `double[]`, is P-84's decision.
- **Applies:** To the compiled path's code generator and run time, for `RR64` values and arrays of them. Limits: the entry requires doubles only. It does not say whether other numbers (`RR32`, the integer types) must be unboxed too, though its reason ("cannot box its numbers") covers them all.
- **Requires:** A worker must treat unboxed doubles as a requirement, not an optional optimisation. Array storage follows P-84.
- **Unfinished:** All of it. The code generator boxes every number today.
- **Could not resolve:**
  - "row lift": a term I lack. It is a microGPT kernel, and the skill does not describe it. (It does not block the decision.)
  - "How arrays store doubles, as `double[]`, is P-84's decision": two readings. (a) P-84 decided that arrays store doubles as `double[]`. (b) P-84 decides the storage, and `double[]` is the form under question. I lean to (a).
  - Where "unboxed" must hold is not stated: in locals, fields, parameters, return values, and inside the specialised classes of generics (SKILL says a number stays boxed "also inside a specialised class"). I cannot tell whether the requirement covers all of these, or only arithmetic and array storage.

**Each entry:**

The type group, the part of the team that built the type checker and the compiler, then worked to make the language run, with performance as the goal and specialization a must, and learned what is feasible. $\begin{array}{l}
{\it add}\ob{X <:{\tt Ring}\ob{X}}(X,X) : X~(*){\it def1}\\
{\it add}\ob{Y <: {\tt Field}\ob{Y}}(Y,Y) : Y~(*){\it def2}\\

- F-225 **In a self-typed trait with no `comprises` clause, or one that lists only `...`, the compiled checker types `self` in the method bodies as `C[\X\] & X`, the trait met with the implementing type, read from the trait's F-bound; the methods' signatures keep `self` at the plain trait type `C[\X\]`, save in the overloading check's exclusion test (F-277), and the checker refuses an extender at another type.** It builds P-146. A self-typed trait is a trait `C[\X\]` whose parameter `X` extends `C[\X\]`. The checker also takes a parameter bounded by a self-typed trait that the trait extends at that parameter, as the team's `Containment` mixins are: a default of the coordinator's. In a trait whose `comprises` clause lists types, `self` is instead the trait met with the union of those types, and the exclusion test reads its signatures plain. For example, `object Bad extends Integral[\ZZ32\]` is refused, since `Bad` is not a `ZZ32`. The rule accepts every self-typed body of the library but `Integral`'s `numerator`, which each integer type declares instead (P-146). Walk has no such rule and loads what it refuses. #!/usr/bin/env python3
"""near.py: the curator's messages in a window before a UTC time, each with the coordinating
session's message that it answered, found along the transcript's reply chain.

    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z            window 60 minutes before the time
    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z 15m        or 2h, 1d
    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z 15m --cut 2000
                                                        cut each printed text at 2000 characters
                                                        (his and the coordinator's), saying so;
                                                        by default every text is printed whole

For each message of his: its time, source (main, s1, queued: see show.py), session, length and
full text. Then the message he answered: the coordinator's turn that his message follows on the
reply chain (tlib.py says how the chain is read), every text of that turn whole, each with its
time and the file and line it was read from (the first copy, when a resumed transcript replays
it). Before it, one line for each turn the chain passed over as not addressed to him (replies to
Stop-hook feedback, to an agent's message or hand-back, to a task notification or check-in, to a
system reminder), and for each text written after he sent his message; a passed-over turn that
answers a notification and ends with an ask to him (a question mark, "The ask", "I recommend",
"your yes", ...) is marked, and the newest such turn printed whole, since he may have answered
it. When he quotes lines ("> ..."), the text on the chain that holds them is named, and printed
whole if it is not the answer. After it, the last lines of the three turns to him further back
on the chain, for a message that answers an older question. A queued message (sent while a turn
ran) starts at its delivery into the turn; texts written after he sent it are not taken. A
message on no chain the index holds (a queued one never delivered) falls back to the time: the
coordinator's last text before it, passing over replies to Stop-hook feedback.
"""
import os
import re
import sys

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
import tlib  # noqa: E402


def cut(s, n):
    if not n or len(s) <= n:
        return s
    return s[:n] + '\n[... cut: %d more characters]' % (len(s) - n)

$\begin{array}{l}
{\it add}\ob{X}({\tt Ring}\ob{X}, {\tt Ring}\ob{X}) :{\tt Ring}\ob{X}~(*){\it def1}\\
{\it add}\ob{Y}({\tt Field}\ob{Y},{\tt Field}\ob{Y}) : {\tt Field}\ob{Y}~(*){\it def2}\\
\end{array}$\\

Take type $\mathbb{Z}$ which is provided as the inputs to {\it add}.  Both {\it def1} and {\it def2}
are applicable.  But if we instantiate {\it def1}
at $\mathbb{Z}$, then we have a return type of ${\tt Ring}\ob{\mathbb{Z}}$ for the less specific
definition.  The more specific {\it def2} is only applicable when instantiated at $\mathbb{Q}$, but the
resulting return type ${\tt Field}\ob{\mathbb{Q}}$ is not a subtype of ${\tt Ring}\ob{\mathbb{Z}}$,
thus witnessing the failure of the return type rule.

Recall that the return type rule handles two failure cases: first, the possibility that more specific
type information at runtime will cause a more specific function definition to be chosen.  Second
is that the more specific function may not be visible to the compiler (hidden behind an API).  Note
that the first failure case should not actually apply here.  When we statically know that we have
a ${\tt Ring}\ob{\mathbb{Z}}$, we actually know much more than this.  The self-type idiom means
that this type is equivalent to $\mathbb{Z}$.  But $\mathbb{Z} <: \mathbb{Q} <: {\tt Field}\ob{\mathbb{Q}}$
which implies that based on static information {\it def2} should apply.  However, this does not extend to
the second failure case when the more specific definition is hidden.

One way to ensure that the first situation cannot happen is to rewrite the overload so that the self-type
